{"id": "72:19/q03", "question": "What is conveyed by calling him 'God's servant'?", "turns_on": "The notes variously stress humility, honor, the reason for worship, the obviousness of serving God, or exact transmission.", "positions": [{"id": "72:19/q03/p1", "position": "It expresses the Prophet's humility and honored, complete servitude to God.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī and al-Rāzī discuss humble self-reference. Bursevī says ʿAbd Allāh is a beloved name, tied to the Night Journey (17:1), the Criterion (25:1), and unmatched servitude; a Persian couplet contrasts it with kings. Ālūsī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, Iṣlāḥī, Kuranyolu and Study Quran see honor or the highest spiritual station in this title; al-Sāmarrāʾī defines chosen servitude as devotion to God's pleasure."}, {"id": "72:19/q03/p2", "position": "The title shows that a servant worshipping his own Lord is natural and gives no cause for hostile amazement.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī contrast rational worship with the opposition it drew. Al-Biqāʿī says worship of another would be the astonishing act, and even an ordinary master's servant should not be treated this way. Iṣlāḥī notes opposition even in the house built for God's worship."}, {"id": "72:19/q03/p3", "position": "The title identifies servanthood as the reason he stood to worship.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī and Bursevī make the title the cause of his standing; al-Ālūsī says it suits an obedient transmission of revelation. Ṭabāṭabāʾī sees preparation for 'I invoke my Lord' in the next verse."}, {"id": "72:19/q03/p4", "position": "The Prophet conveys God's own third-person wording without inserting himself.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says this removes any trace of personal intervention from the transmitted account."}]}
{"id": "72:19/q04", "question": "What does qāma mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the standing denotes the observed prayer or rising to undertake public proclamation.", "positions": [{"id": "72:19/q04/p1", "position": "He stood or rose for prayer and worship.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī gives the bodily upright posture as the root sense. Reports set the action at prayer, often the dawn prayer at Nakhlah. Al-Qāshānī gives the inward equivalent as the heart's turning toward truth."}, {"id": "72:19/q04/p2", "position": "He undertook the public call or mission to God's oneness.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī notes qāma for undertaking a call and also for an event's arising, like the Hour. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 18:14, al-Nābighah's line about the sons of Asad, and Juzʾ ibn Kulayb's verse about the Prophet's public worship. Al-Ḥasan places Arab opposition when he proclaimed monotheism."}]}
{"id": "72:19/q05", "question": "What does yadʿūhu mean, and whom was he addressing?", "turns_on": "Whether yadʿūhu describes worship directed to God or preaching directed to an audience; the reported audience also varies.", "positions": [{"id": "72:19/q05/p1", "position": "He invoked and worshipped God, including through prayer and recitation.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Qurṭubī and al-Bayḍāwī explicitly gloss the verb as worship; al-Samīn describes invocation in monotheism. Al-Ālūsī and Bursevī make it circumstantial to his standing, at the dawn prayer in Nakhlah. Ibn ʿĀshūr takes 'I only call upon my Lord' in 72:20 as its explanation."}, {"id": "72:19/q05/p2", "position": "He called people to God and proclaimed His oneness.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba says he called people to God; al-Ṭabarī and al-Ḥasan specify 'there is no god but God.' Ibn ʿAbbās glosses it as calling people to Him; Ibn ʿĀshūr describes public monotheistic proclamation."}, {"id": "72:19/q05/p3", "position": "He called the jinn to God.", "reasons": "Ibn Jurayj is reported by al-Qurṭubī; the verse's jinn scene gives the proposed addressees."}, {"id": "72:19/q05/p4", "position": "He called the Jews to God.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī transmits this from Ibn Jurayj."}]}
{"id": "72:19/q06", "question": "How does yadʿūhu function grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "72:19/q06/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial clause describing the servant as he stood, invoking God.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn, Bursevī and al-Ālūsī give this parse; Bursevī links the action to Fajr prayer at Nakhlah."}]}
{"id": "72:19/q07", "question": "Who are 'they,' and why did they nearly gather over him?", "turns_on": "The pronoun's antecedent and the motive for gathering: listening, following in prayer, or hostile opposition.", "positions": [{"id": "72:19/q07/p1", "position": "The listening jinn crowded around Muhammad in eagerness, wonder, and love for the Qur'an and his worship.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Zubayr and others give this account. Some say they nearly climbed over him or one another, approached unseen until Gabriel disclosed them (72:1), or marveled at unfamiliar prayer and recitation. Al-Ālūsī says the image implies a larger audience than nine; Bursevī replies that seven or nine at Nakhlah make a crowd unlikely, though approach from one direction could explain it."}, {"id": "72:19/q07/p2", "position": "The Prophet's Companions crowded near him, following his prayer and showing remarkable obedience.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr say they matched his bowing and prostration, and jinn told their people of it. Al-Ṭabrisī adds that each wanted to hear and be closest. Al-Biqāʿī compares an envoy's account of orderly Muslim rows impressing a Persian king. Bursevī says few companions, perhaps only Zayd, were with him and objects to a literal crowd."}, {"id": "72:19/q07/p3", "position": "Arab or Quraysh polytheists crowded around Muhammad in hostility to his monotheistic call.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī prefers this from the link with 72:18: opposition follows the ban on invoking another. Al-Ḥasan describes united Arabs, and Ibn ʿĀshūr derives the referent from 72:16–18; they gathered angrily to hear and intended harm. Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers mockery and loud interruption. Asad broadens it to a recurring majority's hostility to unpopular moral truth."}, {"id": "72:19/q07/p4", "position": "Humans and jinn jointly massed against Muhammad to extinguish his mission, but God supported it.", "reasons": "Qatāda is the recurring authority, often with al-Ḥasan and Ibn Zayd; al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr prefer this hostile reading. Elmalılı says it fits either hamza reading and 72:13. Kuranyolu cites Ṭabarī's preference; Asad relates it to 9:32."}, {"id": "72:19/q07/p5", "position": "Noah's disbelieving people nearly attacked him.", "reasons": "This depends on identifying the servant as Noah; Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī call that identification strained or remote."}, {"id": "72:19/q07/p6", "position": "In an inward reading, the faculties crowd the heart and veil it by their dominance.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī interprets the servant as the heart."}, {"id": "72:19/q07/p7", "position": "Truth-deniers repeatedly mass against any individual or minority defending an unpopular moral truth.", "reasons": "Asad acknowledges Muhammad and his contemporaries as an initial setting, then generalizes the pattern."}]}
{"id": "72:19/q08", "question": "What setting and further events are reported for this scene?", "turns_on": "The transmitted locations, prayer times, and numbers differ.", "positions": [{"id": "72:19/q08/p1", "position": "At Nakhlah, jinn heard Muhammad praying and reciting, then gathered to listen.", "reasons": "Al-Muqātil places him between Mecca and Ṭāʾif with nine jinn; al-Zubayr specifies evening prayer, while al-Zajjāj, al-Zamakhsharī and others specify dawn. Al-Biqāʿī says jinn sent toward Tihāmah by Iblīs heard his monotheism and believed. Ibn Kathīr says he did not see their approach until Gabriel informed him."}, {"id": "72:19/q08/p2", "position": "He prayed and recited in a valley of Mecca.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī gives this location without specifying Nakhlah."}, {"id": "72:19/q08/p3", "position": "At al-Ḥajūn, an Ibn Masʿūd account describes black men like the Zutt crowding around the Prophet after he drew Ibn Masʿūd a line.", "reasons": "Al-Durr transmits the account as before the Hijra; Bursevī says Ibn Masʿūd's event followed Nakhlah and objects that it was witnessed rather than revealed and too few Companions were present."}, {"id": "72:19/q08/p4", "position": "Seventy thousand jinn pledged allegiance or followed the Prophet until daybreak.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī transmits Burd from Makḥūl without grading; al-Biqāʿī cites Makḥūl from Abū Ḥayyān."}]}
{"id": "72:19/q09", "question": "What does libadan mean here?", "turns_on": "The notes offer a physical crowd image, helpers, abundance, endurance, and other related lexical usages.", "positions": [{"id": "72:19/q09/p1", "position": "Dense, layered crowds or heaps packed tightly together.", "reasons": "The singular is libda/lubda; comparisons include felted wool, matted hair and a lion's mane, and a locust swarm. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Wāḥidī cite ʿAbd Manāf's locust verse and explain jābiya as consuming or gathering food; Ibn ʿAṭiyya also records jāni. Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī and al-Rāzī cite Zuhayr's lion line; Dhū al-Rumma is also cited. Ibn Qutayba uses an accumulation of illicit gain. Al-Farrāʾ likens the form to plural human adjectives. Al-Naḥḥās favors the crowd sense over mere abundance and traces the root to accumulated, sticking material, including a mass of hair."}, {"id": "72:19/q09/p2", "position": "Helpers or supporters.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās supplies this gloss in al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Naḥḥās, al-Māwardī and al-Durr; Abū Ḥayyān also reports it."}, {"id": "72:19/q09/p3", "position": "Abundance or a great quantity.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās reports Mujāhid's alternate abundance gloss but favors gathered crowds. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī points to 90:6 and says the ḍamma form suggests numerous listeners, though kasra is more familiar here. Al-Mubarrad calls a similar form 'many' or a singular descriptive form. Al-Qurṭubī also cites abundant wealth."}, {"id

<<chunk 221, part 1 of 0..5>>
": "72:19/q09/p4", "position": "Enduring, like Luqmān's last vulture Lubad.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī cites al-Nābighah's poetry and the lore of Luqmān choosing seven vultures instead of ewes for long life; al-Samīn mentions the name."}, {"id": "72:19/q09/p5", "position": "In another usage, al-labad is a stay-at-home person.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports Abū ʿUbayd's preferred transmitted variant in a line praising good judgment and large undertakings."}, {"id": "72:19/q09/p6", "position": "A cited lion poem may refer to its thick mane, though the excerpt does not identify its lexical target.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās gives an unattributed poem of a well-armed lion with mane and unclipped claws."}]}
{"id": "72:19/q10", "question": "How is libadan read and formed?", "turns_on": "The vowel on lām, the vowel or doubling of bāʾ, and the related singular or plural pattern.", "positions": [{"id": "72:19/q10/p1", "position": "The common reading has kasra on lām and fatḥa on bāʾ, generally a plural of libda.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī prefers the city readers' form; Abū ʿUbayda and Abū Ḥātim also prefer it in al-Thaʿlabī. Nāfiʿ, the majority, and most transmissions use it. Al-Farrāʾ and later grammarians say its sense matches the ḍamma reading. Ibn ʿĀshūr instead calls it a collective noun."}, {"id": "72:19/q10/p2", "position": "With ḍamma on lām and a light, open bāʾ, it is a dialectal plural of lubda.", "reasons": "Attributed variously to Ibn Muḥayṣin, Mujāhid, Hishām from Ibn ʿĀmir, and in some accounts Ibn ʿĀmir. Al-Farrāʾ and al-Ṭabarī say it has the same sense as kasra. Ibn Muḥayṣin also has a still bāʾ form. Qiraat-ER says it can emphasize distinct clusters."}, {"id": "72:19/q10/p3", "position": "With ḍamma on both lām and bāʾ, it is related to lubd, lubūd, or lubayd.", "reasons": "Reports attribute this to Abū Ḥaywah, al-Ḥasan, al-Jaḥdarī and others; al-Qushayrī describes lubayd as a small sack. Some parse it as a plural comparable to ṣabūr/ṣubar."}, {"id": "72:19/q10/p4", "position": "With a doubled bāʾ, it is a plural of lābid describing the clustered people.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ compares bowing and prostrating adjective plurals; al-Zajjāj compares rākiʿ/rukkaʿ and ghāzin/ghuzā. Attributions vary among al-Ḥasan, Abū Jaʿfar, al-Jaḥdarī, Abū al-ʿĀliyah and al-Aʿraj. Abū Rajāʾ has an unusual kasra-on-lām doubled variant."}, {"id": "72:19/q10/p5", "position": "A proposed analysis treats a related labad form as a singular descriptive adjective rather than a plural.", "reasons": "Al-Mubarrad compares ḥaṭam for a person; al-Samīn applies this to the ḍamma form and cites 90:6."}]}
{"id": "72:19/q11", "question": "How does this statement connect with the surrounding verses?", "turns_on": "How the clause's speaker and crowd relate to 72:1, 72:18, and the commands that follow.", "positions": [{"id": "72:19/q11/p1", "position": "It continues the revelation or jinn report begun at 72:1.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī connects a jinn listening account with 72:1. Ibn ʿAṭiyya coordinates the fatḥ reading with 72:1; al-Ṭabrisī and Ibn ʿĀshūr likewise connect it to revelation. Al-Biqāʿī sets both possibilities alongside each other."}, {"id": "72:19/q11/p2", "position": "It follows 72:18's command of exclusive worship by showing hostility to God's servant who obeyed it.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī uses this link to prefer hostile Arabs; al-Ālūsī calls it an elegant transition. Ibn ʿĀshūr traces polytheists through 72:16–18; Iṣlāḥī notes tawḥīd was opposed in the house built for it."}, {"id": "72:19/q11/p3", "position": "The following commands clarify the Prophet's call and God's protection.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says 72:20 explains yadʿūhu. Ṭabāṭabāʾī reads mission, oneness, resurrection and protection from error across these verses; Elmalılı says the commands fit their flow. Al-Ālūsī links 72:21–22 to bodily prostration points. Al-Fārisī compares qāla with imperative qul in 72:20, the latter fitting commands in 21–22."}, {"id": "72:19/q11/p4", "position": "The passage informs the Prophet of unseen outward events and inward feelings.", "reasons": "Elmalılı gives this as a function shared by its interpretive alternatives."}, {"id": "72:19/q11/p5", "position": "Asad connects its recurring opposition to 19:73–74.", "reasons": "He directs readers to those verses and their notes."}]}
{"id": "72:19/q12", "question": "What other lessons do these sources attach to the surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "Whether the gathering is praiseworthy or hostile, with further lessons noted for the passage.", "positions": [{"id": "72:19/q12/p1", "position": "Uprightness may bring Paradise and expanded provision.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī states both possible rewards."}, {"id": "72:19/q12/p2", "position": "The passage calls for reflection on proofs.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī makes this demand explicit."}, {"id": "72:19/q12/p3", "position": "The densely gathered crowd could be praise or blame.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī allows both evaluations of the phrase."}]}
{"id": "72:19/q13", "question": "What do the cited passages say about literary clarity?", "turns_on": "The surrounding literary discussion contrasts a clear image with obscure construction.", "positions": [{"id": "72:19/q13/p1", "position": "The cited verse pictures distinguished men admitted by their standing, while mere approach does not secure entry.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī uses the image of kings' gates."}, {"id": "72:19/q13/p2", "position": "Obscure verbal order makes meaning needlessly indirect; effort pleases only when the discovered meaning merits it.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī likens unrewarding complexity to a miser's empty promises and faults Abū Tammām's strained diction. His line about a 'second' in the sky and two men in the cave illustrates the contrivance."}]}
{"id": "72:19/q14", "question": "What grammatical and recitational principles appear in ancillary citations?", "turns_on": "The citations concern distinct grammatical examples.", "positions": [{"id": "72:19/q14/p1", "position": "A full pause can separate utterances; a lesser pause permits only breath or no interval.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī gives the distinctions."}, {"id": "72:19/q14/p2", "position": "A pronoun of affair is third-person nominative and may introduce a clause without an antecedent.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī reports grammarians parsing huwa with Allāh as second subject and aḥad as predicate; he distinguishes a separation pronoun, which may have any person and case."}, {"id": "72:19/q14/p3", "position": "A poetic example uses masculine agreement with Barada's water.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī says agreement with an overt feminine noun would take feminine tāʾ."}]}
{"id": "72:19/q15", "question": "What ancillary reports address revelation and the seven revealed forms?", "turns_on": "The ancillary reports differ in topic and detail.", "positions": [{"id": "72:19/q15/p1", "position": "The Prophet showed physical effects when revelation came.", "reasons": "ʿĀʾishah describes his head drooping, face changing color, cold teeth, and pearl-like sweat."}, {"id": "72:19/q15/p2", "position": "Each of seven revealed forms is sufficient and should not be abandoned or disputed.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd rejects abandoning one form out of disdain; Abū Bakrah permits any form so long as punishment and mercy are not interchanged; ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ calls disputes over forms unbelief. ʿUthmān confirms witnesses to the Prophet's declaration."}, {"id": "72:19/q15/p3", "position": "The seven-forms report is widely transmitted and raises questions of occasion, meaning, number, and variation.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayd calls it mutawātir. Ibn al-Jazarī traces nineteen Companions and al-Suyūṭī counts twenty-one; Ibn al-Jazarī lays out ten questions."}]}
{"id": "72:20/q01", "question": "How is the opening word read?", "turns_on": "Whether the opening is a direct command, fitting following commands, or a past report continuing the preceding narration; the attributed readers and manuscript observation are also cited.", "positions": [{"id": "72:20/q01/p1", "position": "Qul, an imperative commanding the Prophet to say the declaration.", "reasons": "Farrāʾ reports al-Aʿmash, ʿĀṣim, and most Medinan readers with this form. Ibn Khālawayh says dropping the alif preserves God's direct command. Fārisī connects it to repeated commands in 72:21–22; Wāḥidī, Bayḍāwī, and Ālūsī also cite what follows. Wāḥidī cites Muqātil's report of revelation in response to the Meccans. Reported reader lists vary: ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah recur; Abū Jaʿfar appears in Jishumī, Baghawī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr; Abū ʿAmr is reported by Fārisī, Abū Ḥayyān, and Ālūsī in one transmission. Ibn ʿĀshūr makes it a fresh part of the revelation, with an implied 'it was revealed to me ... then say.' Samīn notes parallels at 17:93, 21:4, and 23:118. Nashr groups Abū Jaʿfar, ʿĀṣim, and Ḥamzah together as readers of the imperative qul without alif."}, {"id": "72:20/q01/p2", "position": "Qāla, a past-tense report that he said the declaration.", "reasons": "Farrāʾ transmits this from ʿAlī. Fārisī says it continues the preceding third-person narration; Ibn Khālawayh says retaining the alif reports that the Prophet first obeyed and then told of it. Wāḥidī, Baghawī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr take the speaker as the Messenger or servant; Wāḥidī says it answers the opponents' demand. Most readers or the remaining readers are assigned this form by several sources; Samīn reports al-Jaḥdarī's observation that the manuscript has qāla. Qirāʾāt-ER says the quoted content stays the same."}]}

Ibn ʿĀshūr says the past-tense reading explains the servant's preceding act of calling upon God."}, {"id": "72:20/q02/p2", "position": "It can begin a fresh clause, and the following clause can also stand independently.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās explicitly allows independence for both. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the imperative reading starts a new revealed instruction, supplied as 'it was revealed to me ... then say.'"}]}
{"id": "72:20/q03", "question": "What account of a negative use of inna is reported?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "72:20/q03/p1", "position": "Some deny negative inna and supply an omitted mā in comparable expressions.", "reasons": "Burhān cites the example mā in al-kāfirūn illā fī ghurūr and a line of poetry in support of omission."}]}
{"id": "72:20/q04", "question": "What does 'I call upon my Lord' mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "72:20/q04/p1", "position": "The Prophet invokes and worships his Lord alone, relying on Him and seeking His protection.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyyah explicitly glosses adʿū as 'I worship.' Qurṭubī and Nasafī explain exclusive invocation and worship. Ibn Kathīr adds seeking refuge and relying on God alone. Elmālili adds that God is his Creator and Lord and that he neither hopes nor fears in another. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the restriction excludes worship of anyone besides God. Biqāʿī names Wadd, Suwāʿ, and Yaghūth among excluded partners, whether idol or living being."}]}
{"id": "72:20/q05", "question": "What point does this declaration make to those who opposed or wondered at him?", "turns_on": "The notes give different emphases for the audience's reaction: hostility to exclusive worship and suspicion of worldly designs.", "positions": [{"id": "72:20/q05/p1", "position": "Worship of God alone is ordinary and gives no cause for amazement, disgust, blame, or united hostility.", "reasons": "Kashshāf says the Prophet does nothing strange; Bayḍāwī, Bursawī, and Ālūsī likewise deny that exclusive worship warrants wonder or collective opposition. Nasafī applies this to the jinn's crowding and amazement. Abū Ḥayyān reports the hostile crowd explanation, with amazed jinn as another audience. Ibn Kathīr describes opponents joining to defeat the truth; Bursawī adds that others should adopt this state. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the audience was bewildered by worship unlike what it had seen; worship of one's recognized Lord deserves no blame. Elmālili and Iṣlāḥī mention hostile opponents' surprise or disgust."}, {"id": "72:20/q05/p2", "position": "He disavows the worldly schemes and tricks that his audience suspects.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī says his sole purpose is to worship his Lord."}]}
{"id": "72:20/q06", "question": "How is the yāʾ of 'my Lord' pronounced?", "turns_on": "The vowel or lack of vowel on the yāʾ.", "positions": [{"id": "72:20/q06/p1", "position": "The yāʾ is opened.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyyah records the difference without naming readers here."}, {"id": "72:20/q06/p2", "position": "The yāʾ is quiescent.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyyah records the difference without naming readers here."}]}
{"id": "72:20/q07", "question": "What does the denial of association exclude?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "72:20/q07/p1", "position": "It excludes every partner in worship alongside God.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī and Nasafī state the denial directly. Biqāʿī includes Wadd, Suwāʿ, and Yaghūth, and says a partner could be an idol or living being. Iṣlāḥī says opponents assign partners a share with God, but the Prophet refuses them."}]}
{"id": "72:20/q08", "question": "Why add an explicit denial of association after the exclusive call?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "72:20/q08/p1", "position": "It reinforces the restriction and gives the denial special emphasis.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the restriction already means worship of God alone; separate wording stresses the exclusion of any partner."}]}
{"id": "72:20/q09", "question": "How is a moving hamza after yāʾ or wāw handled here?", "turns_on": "Whether yāʾ or wāw is intrinsic or added for lengthening or liaison, and whether a long letter can be ignored in easing the hamza.", "positions": [{"id": "72:20/q09/p1", "position": "Transfer and assimilation are both transmitted even when the preceding long letter is additional.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī says readers who ease the corresponding category after alif apply both treatments after yāʾ or wāw, intrinsic or added, including liaison forms; he says analogy would require only assimilation."}, {"id": "72:20/q09/p2", "position": "Transfer is used with yāʾ and wāw generally, but added lengthening or liaison letters take assimilation only.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī prefers this distinction, following Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Ṣāʾigh."}, {"id": "72:20/q09/p3", "position": "The hamza can be eased as if it followed a vowel, ignoring the preceding long letter.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī attributes this extension to Abū al-ʿAlāʾ alone and says reciters and grammarians do not know it."}]}
{"id": "72:20/q10", "question": "What inward practice does exclusive calling entail?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "72:20/q10/p1", "position": "Affirm God's oneness and turn away from everything else to avoid association.", "reasons": "Qāshānī gives this as the inner sense of calling only the Lord."}]}

{"id": "74:12/q04", "question": "What inward meaning is given to the wealth and its recipient?", "turns_on": "Whether the extension concerns inward appetite or a symbolic account of the rebellious self.", "positions": [{"id": "74:12/q04/p1", "position": "God extended al-Walīd's greed and long expectation.", "reasons": "Tustarī gives this inward explanation while naming al-Walīd."}, {"id": "74:12/q04/p2", "position": "The solitary evil soul and its wealth represent bad traits, followers, prestige, sins, and dark natural powers.", "reasons": "The Najmī allusion reported by Bursawī makes al-Walīd this soul; Abū Bakr as the hidden, ʿUmar as spirit, ʿUthmān as secret, and ʿAlī as heart use spiritual light to erase darkness, defeat its acts and followers, and end its rule."}]}
{"id": "74:12/q05", "question": "How is this gift of wealth placed in the surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "Which surrounding frame the note emphasizes: the sequence of gifts, the warning, or a possible parallel in another sūra.", "positions": [{"id": "74:12/q05/p1", "position": "The specific gift of wealth follows the general gift of creating him and begins a rehearsal of blessings before reproach.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the blessings prepare a warning of worldly harm and punishment in the afterlife."}, {"id": "74:12/q05/p2", "position": "Verses 11–17 warn disbelievers that Judgment Day will be severe despite their expectation of more wealth and rank.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says God gave wealth and status, after which the man became conceited and vain; wealthy leaders of Mecca and Ṭāʾif took riches as evidence that God favored them. He compares al-Muddaththir with the preceding al-Muzzammil: similar names and central themes."}, {"id": "74:12/q05/p3", "position": "The blessings here contrast with the vices described in 68:10.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says 68:10 may refer to al-Walīd, but treats this as possible because that context warns against his harm and treachery."}]}
{"id": "74:12/q06", "question": "What does the divine grant of wealth teach about blessings and gratitude?", "turns_on": "Whether the lesson is framed as gratitude owed or the mistaken inference people draw from prosperity.", "positions": [{"id": "74:12/q06/p1", "position": "Abundant blessings make disobedience to their giver more serious and call for gratitude.", "reasons": "Jishumī says the abundance heightens culpability. Kuranyolu says gratitude follows from reason and justice; al-Walīd's ingratitude toward God and the Prophet and efforts to suppress Islam illustrate the fault. Iṣlāḥī says conceit replaced gratitude."}, {"id": "74:12/q06/p2", "position": "Worldly wealth and status can prompt a mistaken claim to divine favor and an expectation of still more.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī describes affluent leaders of Mecca and Ṭāʾif, says Muhammad should leave their fate to God, and takes the passage to apply to al-Walīd and the broader wealthy elite."}]}
{"id": "74:12/q07", "question": "Can God grant worldly blessings to unbelievers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:12/q07/p1", "position": "Yes; worldly goods and conditions are blessings from God even when granted to unbelievers.", "reasons": "Jishumī explicitly disputes the Mujbira on this point and calls worldly conditions and goods divine blessings."}]}
